# Archaeology of North Korea

Archaeology of North Korea encompasses the study of human material remains within the present-day territory of the Democratic People’s Republic of Korea (DPRK), from the earliest prehistory through historic and early modern periods. Research has identified Paleolithic cave and terrace sites, Neolithic settlements and shell middens with pottery traditions, Bronze Age megalithic dolmen contexts, Iron Age hillforts and protohistoric settlements, and extensive remains of historic polities, notably the Goguryeo (often rendered Koguryo in DPRK and UNESCO sources) and Balhae (Bohai) states, along with later Goryeo and Joseon-period heritage found in the North. The Complex of Koguryo Tombs—about 30 mural and other tombs spanning multiple clusters around Pyongyang—was inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List on July 7, 2004, for its outstanding architectural and artistic value and as a record of Goguryeo society; the Historic Monuments and Sites in Kaesong, a serial ensemble of 12 components associated with the Goryeo capital, was inscribed on June 23, 2013 . Archaeological practice in the DPRK operates within a distinct institutional and legal framework, with limited access for foreign researchers and constrained publication visibility. External assessments have noted interpretive and methodological differences compared to neighboring countries, and several long-running scholarly debates concern the location and interpretation of Han dynasty Lelang commandery remains, the framing of Goguryeo heritage across DPRK/ROK/PRC scholarship, and the dating or authenticity of specific finds . The term “Goguryeo” is widely used in international scholarship, while “Koguryo” is employed in DPRK documents and UNESCO materials; both refer to the same kingdom (ca. third century BCE to 668 CE) .

## Scope and terminology

This article surveys archaeology within the DPRK’s present borders, focusing on physical remains, site sequences, research history, institutions and laws, methods and conservation, major discoveries, and documented controversies. It excludes general political history except where directly relevant to archaeological interpretation, management, or access.

Terminology varies across sources. UNESCO and DPRK documents typically use “Koguryo,” while many international academic works use “Goguryeo”; both designate the same historical state . Balhae is often rendered Bohai in Chinese scholarship.

## Natural and research context

Archaeological investigations in the North have recorded cave sites, river terrace deposits, shell middens, burial mounds, fortifications, urban foundations, palatial platforms, observatories, and religious architecture. The published record is shaped by DPRK institutions and heritage law, selective international collaboration, and UNESCO nomination and monitoring processes for its World Heritage properties . Within the DPRK, archaeology has been linked to national heritage agendas and cultural policy, including the designation of non-physical heritage since 2012 and a broadened legal framework in 2015 and 2019 .

## Periodization and cultural sequence

### Paleolithic

Evidence of Paleolithic occupation includes cave and terrace sites around the Pyongyang region and elsewhere. DPRK announcements and museum displays identify Komunmoru (a cave site near Sangwon) as an early Paleolithic locale; scholarly assessments caution that detailed stratigraphic and dating information from DPRK sources is limited in availability outside the country . DPRK media in July 2019 reported late Paleolithic finds—stone tools, bone implements, and mammal fossils—near the Yesong River in North Hwanghae Province, with electron paramagnetic resonance and thermoluminescence cited in separate DPRK reports for other cave sites; the UPI report attributed these claims to KCNA . A peer-reviewed abstract notes luminescence dating work at the Joohyondong Cave site near Hyangmok-ri (Kangdong County), reflecting the application of physicochemical dating methods to DPRK Neolithic/Paleolithic contexts .

### Neolithic (pottery traditions and subsistence)

On the Korean Peninsula, the Neolithic period features pottery traditions, varying degrees of sedentism, and mixed subsistence including fishing, foraging, and cultivation. A peninsula-wide synthesis of radiocarbon dates shows that shell middens and pit-house settlements proliferated, and that cultivation of broomcorn and foxtail millet is supported by AMS dating by the middle Neolithic; rice impressions in Neolithic pottery are rare or absent in the verified record . The absolute chronology for the earliest pottery tradition (Gosan-ri-type) has been modeled in Korea using radiocarbon and statistical methods, placing its production around the mid-eighth millennium BCE; these results inform comparative sequences that include northern sites . DPRK research has reported Jeulmun (comb-patterned) pottery and shell middens along the Taedong River basin, including early excavations at Unggi/Hoeryong, although detailed, openly accessible excavation reports remain scarce in English .

### Bronze Age (dolmens and associated contexts)

Dolmens are widespread across the Korean Peninsula and are generally associated with Bronze Age societies. UNESCO and ICOMOS describe three typological clusters—table/northern type (above-ground cist under a capstone), go-board/southern type (underground chamber with a capstone supported on ground-laid stones), and variants with capstones laid directly on buried slabs—and outline construction techniques and chronology from the seventh to third centuries BCE based on well-dated southern sites . Dolmens occur extensively within DPRK territory, but site-level distribution and counts are less documented in accessible international literature; comparative typology and chronology are used to frame northern assemblages in relation to peninsula-wide Bronze Age developments .

### Iron Age and protohistoric periods

Asian Perspectives identifies the Early Iron Age in Korea roughly from 300 to 100 BCE, with evidence suggesting iron technology arrived via contact with the Yan polity and spread through trade networks; domestic iron production becomes archaeologically visible by the later first millennium BCE . Archaeological patterns from the fourth century BCE into the early centuries CE show fortified settlements, walled sites, and evolving material culture. Studies of Goguryeo fortification techniques highlight construction features that also appear in late phases after the capital’s relocation to Pyongyang in 427 CE, providing a comparative framework for DPRK fortresses .

### Historic states: Goguryeo and Balhae

Goguryeo originated in the northeastern borderlands and shifted its capital multiple times: to Kungnae Castle (Ji’an) in 3 CE, to the Mt. Taesong area near Pyongyang in 427 CE, and to Jangan Castle in central Pyongyang later in the fifth century; the kingdom fell in 668 CE . Within the DPRK, extensive Goguryeo funerary landscapes include stone-chambered tombs under earthen mounds with complex structural ceilings and mural programs depicting cosmology, processions, and daily life . Balhae (Bohai), a successor state in the northeast, encompassed parts of Northeast China, the northern Korean Peninsula, and the Russian Far East; joint DPRK–China projects and Korean-led research have documented Balhae fortresses and tomb clusters in North Hamgyong Province (Heoryeong) and near Cheongjin .

### Later Goryeo and Joseon remains in the North

The Kaesong area preserves major Goryeo-period monuments and urban features, including city walls, palace terraces, observatory, gates, academies, and royal mausolea; many were repaired or reconstructed under DPRK management. The Kaesong serial property illustrates political and philosophical content of the Goryeo state and later Joseon conservation practices within the DPRK territory .

## Major sites and discoveries

### Complex of Koguryo Tombs (UNESCO World Heritage)

The serial World Heritage property comprises about 30 tombs across multiple clusters around Pyongyang, Nampho, and South Hwanghae Province. The nomination and ICOMOS evaluation emphasize structural innovation in spanning wide chambers, varied burial plans, and mural programs of high artistic quality. The property was inscribed under criteria (i), (ii), (iii), and (iv) .

- Composition and typology: Stone-piled and stone-chambered tombs under earthen mounds; single-, two-, multi-, and side-chambered plans with corridors. Ceilings use corbeling, lantern tiers, and other load-bearing designs to support heavy superstructures .
- Murals and themes: Portraits of occupants, the Four Directional Deities (Azure Dragon, White Tiger, Vermilion Bird, Black Warrior), processions, hunting, dance and music, astronomy (sun with three-legged crow, moon with toad/rabbit, Big Dipper, Milky Way), decorative cloud and lotus motifs; genre scenes record architecture, clothing, instruments, arms, and activities .
- Conservation: Interiors and murals are largely preserved; issues include mural deterioration in some tombs, occasional flooding, and legacy interventions. ICOMOS recommended enhanced monitoring and lighting, interpretive signage, a visitor management plan, and pigment studies; it also noted the desirability of coordination with PRC for broader serial context .

#### Anak Tomb No. 3

Anak Tomb No. 3 (South Hwanghae Province) is one of the most detailed mural tombs and among the few with a dated inscription. The epitaph records completion in 357 CE. The tomb contains portraits of the deceased couple, a corridor procession exceeding 200 figures, and extensive scenes of domestic spaces (e.g., mill, kitchen, carriage shed, stable) and guards with banners and axes, along with lotus motifs and musical performances . Architectural features include an entrance passage, antechamber, two side rooms, a main chamber, and an L-shaped gallery; polished basalt and limestone were used, with murals painted directly on stone using preliminary sketches, polychrome fills, and black ink outlines . Comparative scholarship frames Anak No. 3 within the development of Goguryeo mural themes from mixed genre scenes to later dominance of the Four Deities .

#### Other representative mural tombs and clusters

Scholarly and museum publications describe additional DPRK mural tombs included within or related to the World Heritage property:

- Deokheung-ri Tomb (408 CE, Nampho): Two-chamber layout with a 14-line epitaph identifying an occupant’s biography and burial date; murals include officials, a military procession, the myth of the Oxherd and Weaver, auspicious birds, hunting, and a labeled heavenly horse .
- Yaksu-ri Tomb (early 5th century, Nampho): Mixed genre scenes and Four Deities; large hunting panel; astronomical motifs (sun, moon, seven stars) .
- Ssangyeongchong (“Twin Pillar Tomb,” late 5th century, Nampho): Corridor with octagonal pillars; genre scenes, immortals, processions led by a monk; richly painted ceilings with sun, moon, and lotus .
- Susan-ri Tomb (late 5th century, Nampho): Processions with acrobats; refined female portraits; cross-references to Asuka-period Japanese imagery underscore cultural exchange .
- Honam-ri Sasinchong (“Four Deities Tomb,” early 6th century, Pyongyang): Large marble construction; murals focus solely on the Four Deities, indicating a thematic shift .
- Kangseo Three Tombs (late 6th–early 7th century, Nampho): Masterpieces of the late period with polished Four Deities iconography and rich ceiling auspicious beings and celestial motifs .

### Pyongyang-area historical remains (Tentative List)

The DPRK has placed “Historical Relics in Pyongyang” on UNESCO’s Tentative List, indicating an intention to develop a nomination for urban and monumental heritage associated with Goguryeo capital functions and later periods. Tentative List content is submitted by the State Party and published by UNESCO with a disclaimer that responsibility for its details lies with the State Party . Published World Heritage documentation on the Koguryo Tombs outlines Goguryeo’s capital moves to Mt. Taesong and central Pyongyang, and mentions defensive works of Jangan Castle in the city area .

### Historic Monuments and Sites in Kaesong (UNESCO World Heritage)

The Kaesong serial property consists of 12 components that collectively illustrate the Goryeo capital’s planning, education, defenses, ritual landscapes, and funerary culture . Key components include:

- Kaesong City Walls: An Outer Wall (constructed 1009–1029), Inner Wall (1391–1393), and Palocham Wall (896), reflecting successive urban/rural defensive strategies .
- Manwoldae Palace and Kaesong Chomsongdae Observatory: The palace foundation (established 919) preserves terraces and central halls; the observatory platform is associated with early Goryeo astronomy .
- Namdae Gate: The main south gate of the Inner Wall (1393) features a granite base and reconstructed wooden pavilion housing the 1346 Yonbok Temple bell .
- Educational institutions and bridges: Koryo Songgyungwan (academy), Sungyang Sowon (Confucian academy, 1573), Sonjuk Bridge and Phyochung Monuments (stelae of 1740 and 1872) .
- Royal mausolea: Mausoleum of King Wang Kon (restored exterior in 1994), Mausoleum of King Kongmin and Queen (completed 1372), and the Seven Tombs/Myongrung cluster .

ICOMOS noted legal protection through DPRK law and regulations, a management plan approved in January 2011, and issues such as urban development in buffer zones, heavy summer rains, insect damage risks, and the need for visitor flow management . Inter-Korean joint excavations at Manwoldae have occurred in multiple campaigns, including an extended season in 2015; public reporting and official project pages document finds and collaboration logistics .

### Balhae (Bohai) sites in North Hamgyong

A joint excavation (2012–2013) by the Archaeological Research Institute of the DPRK Academy of Social Sciences and Yanbian University’s Balhae History Institute investigated fortresses (Ingyeri Earthen Fortress, Undu Fortress, Donggeon Fortress) and the Gungsim tomb complex in Heoryeong, North Hamgyong Province, producing a detailed report on site distributions, stratigraphy, and chronology . Additional DPRK publications summarize work at Bugeori (Cheongjin) and link DPRK investigations to broader Northeast Asian Balhae research, including temple sites at Kraskino across the Tumen (Duman) River in Russia; these materials are part of a long-running scholarly effort to define Balhae urban and mortuary landscapes across modern borders .

### Bronze Age dolmen concentrations

UNESCO’s ICOMOS evaluation of the Republic of Korea’s dolmen properties established typological and chronological frameworks applicable to peninsula-wide dolmens, including those within DPRK territory. It documented quarrying, transport, and erection techniques and emphasized that Korea has the largest concentration of dolmens known worldwide; comparative notes have suggested the potential for northern dolmen inclusion in future serial nominations when feasible .

### Shell middens, settlements, and material culture

Early DPRK archaeology reported shell middens and mixed-material culture sites in the northeast (Unggi/Hoeryong), with subsequent work across Jeulmun pottery-bearing settlements and Mumun plain pottery contexts; much of the openly accessible synthesis is peninsula-wide, and DPRK site-level excavation data are less available in English-language publications .

## History of archaeological research

### Japanese colonial-era archaeology (pre-1945)

Systematic survey and excavation in northern Korea began under Japanese rule. Colonial-era laws on protection of “ancient remains and relics” were enacted and Governor-General-sponsored committees inventoried and excavated sites, including fortified places and tombs. Colonial scholarship’s emphasis on confirming Han dynasty commandery centers around Pyongyang (especially Lelang) intertwined archaeology with political legitimation . Museum institutions in Pyongyang and Kaesong were established, and materials entered Japanese collections .

### Post-1948 DPRK institutions and campaigns

Archaeology in the DPRK was institutionalized under the Academy of Social Sciences, with an Institute of Archaeology and related museum and cultural preservation bodies. Journals such as Munhwa yusan (1957–1962), Kogo minsok (from 1963), and Joseon gogo yeongu (from 1986) have served as main outlets; a recent bibliometric analysis counted 1,656 articles in Joseon gogo yeongu through 2019 and charted shifts in topical emphasis across leadership eras . Major early postwar projects included excavations of Goguryeo tombs and Bronze/Neolithic sites. Salvage archaeology and restoration accompanied infrastructure and urban works, and DPRK heritage bodies managed repairs and reconstruction at serial properties like Kaesong .

### International collaborations

UNESCO advisory evaluations and periodic reporting have engaged DPRK authorities on Koguryo and Kaesong properties, with recommendations on conservation, monitoring, and management planning . ICOMOS encouraged DPRK and PRC to consider future joint nomination coordination for Goguryeo serial properties across borders . The DPRK has carried out joint excavations on Balhae sites with Chinese institutions in Heoryeong and published reports intended for wider academic use . Inter-Korean archaeological collaboration at Manwoldae in Kaesong has been reported across multiple excavation seasons and institutional channels in 2007 and later, including an extended 2015 season .

### Publication patterns

DPRK archaeology publications have emphasized national heritage, historical continuity, and ideological frameworks, with shifts toward Kaesong and Manwoldae topics noted in recent bibliometric studies. Language barriers and limited distribution mean that many DPRK excavation reports are not widely accessible in English, and external syntheses often rely on UNESCO documentation, inter-Korean project reports, and comparative peninsula-wide research .

## Institutions and legal frameworks

Heritage management in the DPRK is organized through national and local bodies. UNESCO/ICOMOS documentation identifies:

- Management Bureau for Cultural Property Conservation (MBCPC) under the Ministry of Culture, with provincial/city Bureaus of Cultural Preservation, local cultural preservation departments, and Cultural Relics Management Offices (CRMO); site managers and caretakers implement on-site protection and monitoring .
- Legal protection deriving from the Socialist Constitution, specific cultural property laws and regulations, and related environmental and land management laws. The Historic Monuments and Sites in Kaesong nomination cites the Law on Protection of Cultural Property (1994) and its implementing regulations (2009), administered by the National Bureau for Cultural Property Conservation (NBCPC), along with a management plan approved in 2011 .
- Policy evolution since 2012: DPRK enacted a Cultural Heritage Protection law that expanded to intangible heritage, then adopted the Law on the Protection of National Heritage in 2015 (six chapters, 62 clauses; later amended in January 2019 to refine definitions, expand non-physical heritage categories, remove individual ownership, and prioritize excavation, preservation, and economic use). The amended law directs a central institution to pursue UNESCO registrations strategically .

Museums and academic bodies include the Korean Central History Museum (Pyongyang), the Academy of Social Sciences (Institute of Archaeology), and university departments; these institutions conduct research, curation, and public display of excavated materials .

## Methods and technology

DPRK archaeology employs excavation, survey, typology, and laboratory techniques, with documented use of radiocarbon (14C), accelerator mass spectrometry (AMS), and luminescence dating in peninsula-wide studies and in specific DPRK site contexts (e.g., Joohyondong Cave abstract). Asian Perspectives provides radiocarbon datasets and analytical methods for Neolithic sedentism and settlement sequences that inform comparative frameworks inclusive of the DPRK sector . Conservation of mural tombs involves environmental monitoring (hygrometry, temperature), lighting control, and protective measures; ICOMOS recommended enhancing equipment and pigment analysis, installing alarms and protective doors, and developing visitor management plans for serial properties . Museum and research publications document pigment palettes (e.g., cinnabar, lead white, ochre, verdigris, carbon ink) and iconographic programs in mural tombs, contributing to studies of materials and techniques .

## Heritage management and conservation

World Heritage serial properties in the DPRK have defined management systems, legal protections, and monitoring protocols. For Koguryo Tombs, ICOMOS noted authenticity of interiors and murals, identified specific risks (deterioration, flooding), and recommended research and visitor management actions; UNESCO’s documents page records periodic reporting and mission follow-ups . The Kaesong property’s management plan sets conservation priorities for walls, gates, palatial terraces, academies, and mausolea, with legal backing from DPRK cultural property laws and buffer zone guidelines; ICOMOS identified potential adverse visual impacts from ancillary facilities and stressed mitigation of environmental threats . DPRK official media report periodic restoration activities (e.g., repairs to temples, mausolea, and city walls; tree planting; insect monitoring), and national heritage promotion months, reflecting public heritage campaigns .

## Access, data limitations, and reliability

Access to DPRK sites for foreign researchers is limited, and DPRK publications are not widely distributed internationally. UNESCO publishes State Party nomination files and evaluations but notes that content in national submissions is the responsibility of the submitting State and does not imply positions on legal status or boundaries . External analyses highlight ideological framing and nationalist narratives within DPRK archaeology and caution about verification challenges; paleolithic claims have been critiqued for limited evidentiary support in openly accessible datasets, and the use of traditional accounts for chronological claims has been noted . Bibliometric work demonstrates sustained domestic scholarly output, but language and access constraints impede comprehensive external review .

## Scholarly debates and controversies

- Goguryeo heritage across borders: Because Goguryeo sites and mural tombs span present-day DPRK and PRC territories (Ji’an region), interpretive disputes and heritage claims have involved institutions in both countries. UNESCO inscribed separate serial properties in 2004 and encouraged dialogue on future joint nomination possibilities .
- Lelang commandery: Archaeological and historical evidence supports a Han dynasty commandery centered near Pyongyang from 108 BCE; some DPRK scholarship has contested this localization. Hyung Il Pai’s World Archaeology study analyzes the material record—seals, mirrors, jades, ornaments—within an acculturation framework, providing a methodological reference point for debates on commandery presence and cultural dynamics .
- Dangun mausoleum and early claims: External observers have cited DPRK uses of archaeology in national historiography, including strong critiques of claims surrounding the Dangun mausoleum; the ISDP study surveys paleolithic and early state narratives and their political contexts .

## Recent developments up to 2025

UNESCO’s documents page for the Koguryo Tombs records periodic reporting cycles, including submissions in the 2012 and 2023 cycles, and advisory follow-ups on conservation and management issues . Inter-Korean excavations continued at Manwoldae in Kaesong, with notable collaborative seasons reported publicly in 2015 and institutional pages documenting joint work and findings . DPRK heritage policy evolved through amendments to the Law on the Protection of National Heritage in January 2019, refining definitions and management of non-physical heritage and emphasizing UNESCO registration strategies . DPRK media have reported ongoing maintenance and restoration works at heritage sites, including Kaesong municipal actions and national heritage promotion periods .

## Notes on names and transliteration

Romanization of Korean place names varies by system (Revised Romanization, McCune–Reischauer) and across DPRK, ROK, and international usage; UNESCO and DPRK materials often render names in DPRK transliteration (e.g., “Koguryo,” “Nampho”), while international academic works may use “Goguryeo,” “Nampo.” This article follows the spellings used in cited sources and notes widely accepted variants where helpful .

Ssangyeongchong features genre scenes, immortals, and processions led by a monk.
Ssangyeongchong has richly painted ceilings with sun, moon, and lotus.
Susan-ri Tomb (late 5th century, Nampho) features processions with acrobats.
Susan-ri Tomb contains refined female portraits.
Cross-references to Asuka-period Japanese imagery in Susan-ri Tomb underscore cultural exchange.
Honam-ri Sasinchong (“Four Deities Tomb,” early 6th century, Pyongyang) is a large marble construction.
Murals in Honam-ri Sasinchong focus solely on the Four Deities, indicating a thematic shift.
Kangseo Three Tombs (late 6th–early 7th century, Nampho) are masterpieces of the late period.
Kangseo Three Tombs feature polished Four Deities iconography and rich ceiling auspicious beings and celestial motifs.
The DPRK has placed “Historical Relics in Pyongyang” on UNESCO’s Tentative List.
This indicates an intention to develop a nomination for urban and monumental heritage associated with Goguryeo capital functions and later periods.
Tentative List content is submitted by the State Party and published by UNESCO with a disclaimer that responsibility for its details lies with the State Party.
Published World Heritage documentation on the Koguryo Tombs outlines Goguryeo’s capital moves to Mt. Taesong and central Pyongyang.
The documentation mentions defensive works of Jangan Castle in the city area.
The Kaesong serial property consists of 12 components that collectively illustrate the Goryeo capital’s planning, education, defenses, ritual landscapes, and funerary culture.
Kaesong City Walls include an Outer Wall (constructed 1009–1029), Inner Wall (1391–1393), and Palocham Wall (896).
These walls reflect successive urban/rural defensive strategies.
Manwoldae Palace foundation (established 919) preserves terraces and central halls.
Kaesong Chomsongdae Observatory platform is associated with early Goryeo astronomy.
Namdae Gate is the main south gate of the Inner Wall (1393).
Namdae Gate features a granite base and reconstructed wooden pavilion housing the 1346 Yonbok Temple bell.
Educational institutions and bridges include Koryo Songgyungwan (academy), Sungyang Sowon (Confucian academy, 1573), Sonjuk Bridge and Phyochung Monuments (stelae of 1740 and 1872).
Royal mausolea include the Mausoleum of King Wang Kon (restored exterior in 1994), Mausoleum of King Kongmin and Queen (completed 1372), and the Seven Tombs/Myongrung cluster.
ICOMOS noted legal protection through DPRK law and regulations for the Kaesong property.
ICOMOS noted a management plan approved in January 2011 for the Kaesong property.
ICOMOS noted issues such as urban development in buffer zones, heavy summer rains, insect damage risks, and the need for visitor flow management for the Kaesong property.
Inter-Korean joint excavations at Manwoldae have occurred in multiple campaigns, including an extended season in 2015.
Public reporting and official project pages document finds and collaboration logistics for the Manwoldae excavations.

A joint excavation (2012–2013) by the Archaeological Research Institute of the DPRK Academy of Social Sciences and Yanbian University’s Balhae History Institute investigated fortresses (Ingyeri Earthen Fortress, Undu Fortress, Donggeon Fortress) and the Gungsim tomb complex in Heoryeong, North Hamgyong Province.
The joint excavation produced a detailed report on site distributions, stratigraphy, and chronology.
Additional DPRK publications summarize work at Bugeori (Cheongjin).
DPRK investigations are linked to broader Northeast Asian Balhae research, including temple sites at Kraskino across the Tumen (Duman) River in Russia.
These materials are part of a long-running scholarly effort to define Balhae urban and mortuary landscapes across modern borders.

UNESCO’s ICOMOS evaluation of the Republic of Korea’s dolmen properties established typological and chronological frameworks applicable to peninsula-wide dolmens, including those within DPRK territory.
The evaluation documented quarrying, transport, and erection techniques for dolmens.
The evaluation emphasized that Korea has the largest concentration of dolmens known worldwide.
Comparative notes have suggested the potential for northern dolmen inclusion in future serial nominations when feasible.
Early DPRK archaeology reported shell middens and mixed-material culture sites in the northeast (Unggi/Hoeryong).
Subsequent work occurred across Jeulmun pottery-bearing settlements and Mumun plain pottery contexts.
Much of the openly accessible synthesis is peninsula-wide.
DPRK site-level excavation data are less available in English-language publications.
Systematic survey and excavation in northern Korea began under Japanese rule.
Colonial-era laws on protection of “ancient remains and relics” were enacted.
Governor-General-sponsored committees inventoried and excavated sites, including fortified places and tombs.
Colonial scholarship’s emphasis on confirming Han dynasty commandery centers around Pyongyang (especially Lelang) intertwined archaeology with political legitimation.
Museum institutions in Pyongyang and Kaesong were established.
Materials entered Japanese collections.
Archaeology in the DPRK was institutionalized under the Academy of Social Sciences, with an Institute of Archaeology and related museum and cultural preservation bodies.
Journals such as Munhwa yusan (1957–1962), Kogo minsok (from 1963), and Joseon gogo yeongu (from 1986) have served as main outlets.
A recent bibliometric analysis counted 1,656 articles in Joseon gogo yeongu through 2019.
The bibliometric analysis charted shifts in topical emphasis across leadership eras.
Major early postwar projects included excavations of Goguryeo tombs and Bronze/Neolithic sites.
Salvage archaeology and restoration accompanied infrastructure and urban works.
DPRK heritage bodies managed repairs and reconstruction at serial properties like Kaesong.
UNESCO advisory evaluations and periodic reporting have engaged DPRK authorities on Koguryo and Kaesong properties.
Recommendations on conservation, monitoring, and management planning have been made.
ICOMOS encouraged DPRK and PRC to consider future joint nomination coordination for Goguryeo serial properties across borders.
The DPRK has carried out joint excavations on Balhae sites with Chinese institutions in Heoryeong.
The DPRK has published reports intended for wider academic use.
Inter-Korean archaeological collaboration at Manwoldae in Kaesong has been reported across multiple excavation seasons and institutional channels in 2007 and later, including an extended 2015 season.
DPRK archaeology publications have emphasized national heritage, historical continuity, and ideological frameworks.
Shifts toward Kaesong and Manwoldae topics have been noted in recent bibliometric studies.
Language barriers and limited distribution mean that many DPRK excavation reports are not widely accessible in English.
External syntheses often rely on UNESCO documentation, inter-Korean project reports, and comparative peninsula-wide research.
Heritage management in the DPRK is organized through national and local bodies.
UNESCO/ICOMOS documentation identifies the Management Bureau for Cultural Property Conservation (MBCPC) under the Ministry of Culture.
The MBCPC has provincial/city Bureaus of Cultural Preservation, local cultural preservation departments, and Cultural Relics Management Offices (CRMO).
Site managers and caretakers implement on-site protection and monitoring.
Legal protection derives from the Socialist Constitution, specific cultural property laws and regulations, and related environmental and land management laws.
The Historic Monuments and Sites in Kaesong nomination cites the Law on Protection of Cultural Property (1994) and its implementing regulations (2009).
The Law on Protection of Cultural Property is administered by the National Bureau for Cultural Property Conservation (NBCPC).
A management plan approved in 2011 is cited for the Historic Monuments and Sites in Kaesong.
DPRK enacted a Cultural Heritage Protection law that expanded to intangible heritage since 2012.
The DPRK adopted the Law on the Protection of National Heritage in 2015 (six chapters, 62 clauses).

The Law on the Protection of National Heritage was later amended in January 2019 to refine definitions, expand non-physical heritage categories, remove individual ownership, and prioritize excavation, preservation, and economic use.
The amended law directs a central institution to pursue UNESCO registrations strategically.
Museums and academic bodies include the Korean Central History Museum (Pyongyang), the Academy of Social Sciences (Institute of Archaeology), and university departments.
These institutions conduct research, curation, and public display of excavated materials.
DPRK archaeology employs excavation, survey, typology, and laboratory techniques.

Documented use of radiocarbon (14C), accelerator mass spectrometry (AMS), and luminescence dating occurs in peninsula-wide studies and in specific DPRK site contexts (e.g., Joohyondong Cave abstract).
Asian Perspectives provides radiocarbon datasets and analytical methods for Neolithic sedentism and settlement sequences.
These datasets and methods inform comparative frameworks inclusive of the DPRK sector.
Conservation of mural tombs involves environmental monitoring (hygrometry, temperature), lighting control, and protective measures.
ICOMOS recommended enhancing equipment and pigment analysis, installing alarms and protective doors, and developing visitor management plans for serial properties.
Museum and research publications document pigment palettes (e.g., cinnabar, lead white, ochre, verdigris, carbon ink) and iconographic programs in mural tombs.
These documentations contribute to studies of materials and techniques.
World Heritage serial properties in the DPRK have defined management systems, legal protections, and monitoring protocols.
For Koguryo Tombs, ICOMOS noted authenticity of interiors and murals.
ICOMOS identified specific risks (deterioration, flooding) for Koguryo Tombs.
ICOMOS recommended research and visitor management actions for Koguryo Tombs.
UNESCO’s documents page records periodic reporting and mission follow-ups for Koguryo Tombs.
The Kaesong property’s management plan sets conservation priorities for walls, gates, palatial terraces, academies, and mausolea.
The management plan has legal backing from DPRK cultural property laws and buffer zone guidelines.
ICOMOS identified potential adverse visual impacts from ancillary facilities for the Kaesong property.
ICOMOS stressed mitigation of environmental threats for the Kaesong property.
DPRK official media report periodic restoration activities (e.g., repairs to temples, mausolea, and city walls; tree planting; insect monitoring).
DPRK official media report national heritage promotion months, reflecting public heritage campaigns.
Access to DPRK sites for foreign researchers is limited.
DPRK publications are not widely distributed internationally.
UNESCO publishes State Party nomination files and evaluations.
UNESCO notes that content in national submissions is the responsibility of the submitting State and does not imply positions on legal status or boundaries.
External analyses highlight ideological framing and nationalist narratives within DPRK archaeology.
External analyses caution about verification challenges in DPRK archaeology.
Paleolithic claims have been critiqued for limited evidentiary support in openly accessible datasets.
The use of traditional accounts for chronological claims has been noted.
Bibliometric work demonstrates sustained domestic scholarly output.
Language and access constraints impede comprehensive external review.
Because Goguryeo sites and mural tombs span present-day DPRK and PRC territories (Ji’an region), interpretive disputes and heritage claims have involved institutions in both countries.
UNESCO inscribed separate serial properties in 2004.
UNESCO encouraged dialogue on future joint nomination possibilities.
Archaeological and historical evidence supports a Han dynasty commandery centered near Pyongyang from 108 BCE.
Some DPRK scholarship has contested the localization of the Han dynasty commandery.
Hyung Il Pai’s World Archaeology study analyzes the material record—seals, mirrors, jades, ornaments—within an acculturation framework.
The study provides a methodological reference point for debates on commandery presence and cultural dynamics.
External observers have cited DPRK uses of archaeology in national historiography, including strong critiques of claims surrounding the Dangun mausoleum.
The ISDP study surveys paleolithic and early state narratives and their political contexts.
UNESCO’s documents page for the Koguryo Tombs records periodic reporting cycles, including submissions in the 2012 and 2023 cycles.
The documents page records advisory follow-ups on conservation and management issues.
Inter-Korean excavations continued at Manwoldae in Kaesong, with notable collaborative seasons reported publicly in 2015.
Institutional pages document joint work and findings.
DPRK heritage policy evolved through amendments to the Law on the Protection of National Heritage in January 2019.
The amendments refined definitions and management of non-physical heritage.
The amendments emphasized UNESCO registration strategies.
DPRK media have reported ongoing maintenance and restoration works at heritage sites, including Kaesong municipal actions and national heritage promotion periods.
Romanization of Korean place names varies by system (Revised Romanization, McCune–Reischauer) and across DPRK, ROK, and international usage.
UNESCO and DPRK materials often render names in DPRK transliteration (e.g., “Koguryo,” “Nampho”).
International academic works may use “Goguryeo,” “Nampo.”
This article follows the spellings used in cited sources and notes widely accepted variants where helpful.

# Koguryo Tombs (D. P. R. of Korea) No 1091 1. BASIC DATA 

State Party: Democratic Peoples’ Rep. of Korea 

Name of property: Complex of Koguryo Tombs 

Location: Pyongyang, South Phyongan Province, Nampho, South Hwangghae Province 

Date received: 25 January 2002 

Category of property: 

In terms of the categories of cultural property set out in Article 1 of the 1972 World Heritage Convention, it could be a monument . It is a serial nomination. 

Brief description: 

Several groups and individual tombs from the period of the Koguryo Kingdom. The Koguryo was one of the strongest kingdoms in northeast China and half of the Korean peninsula between the 3 rd century BC and 7 th century AD. These tombs, from the later period of the kingdom, many with beautiful wall paintings, are almost the only remains of this culture. 

2. THE PROPERTY 

Description 

Complexes of tombs, all together consisting of about 30 individual ones, located mainly in agricultural areas and some in villages. Several types of these tombs exist – stone piled, stone chambered and earthen mound tombs. So far over 10,000 tombs belonging to the Koguryo kingdom have been identified, in China and Korea. Among those, some 90 are decorated with wall paintings, 70 of which are in Korea and almost half are the subject of this nomination. These decorated tombs are supposed to be specially made for kings, members of the royal family and other aristocrats. The paintings in the tombs are divided into several types: paintings of portraits, portraits and Four Deities, Four Deities alone, decorative patterns. There are also several types of tombs, according to the number of burial chambers – single chamber, two chamber, multi chamber and side chamber types. They are built of stone and corridors lead into the burial chambers. The tombs have varied shapes of ceilings some quite elaborate, having to solve the need of roofing wide spaces without columns, with stone slabs which had to carry the heavy load of a stone or earth tumulus (mound). 

History 

The Koguryo kingdom existed for nearly 1,000 years, from 277 BC to 668 AD. It was established in Huanren, Liaoning Province in China, relocated in the year 3 AD to Kungnae Castle in Ji’an, Jilin Province, China, to Mt. Taesong area in Pyongyang, in 427 AD and finally to the Jangan Castle in the centre of the present day city of Pyongyang. Pyongyang, situated in a strategic location, had long been the political, economic and cultural centre, as the capital of ancient Korea (Kojoson) which is the reason why the Koguryo kingdom moved its capital here and made great efforts in developing it. The Koguryo kingdom expanded its territory to cover northeast China and half of the Korean peninsula, becoming one of the strongest powers in the east. It collapsed in the year 668 AD. The best known cultural heritage remains of this kingdom are thousands of tombs, built of stone and covered by stone or earthen mounds. Earthen mound tombs, including many with murals, were prevalent once Koguryo moved its capital to Pyongyang – but existed in other parts of the kingdom as well. Most of the known tombs suffered of clandestine excavations in the last thousand years. As a result very few were scientifically excavated prior to such activity and there are very few complete objects coming from the tombs. The tombs received worldwide attention only in 1905, when during the Japanese occupation many of them were opened to the general public. The first scientific research and documentation were carried out by Japanese scholars between 1911 and the 1940s. Regular surveys, excavations and documentation took place from 1945 on. Minor conservation actions took place in early 1940’s, such as restricting entry to tombs and creating entrances to some. Regular maintenance, protection and conservation works started in 1946, with proper legislation and nomination of site managers. 

Management regime 

Legal provision :The main three laws protecting cultural heritage and its management are: Presidential decree 35, ‘Socialist Constitution of the Democratic Peoples’ Rep. of Korea’ and the ‘Law of the Dem. Peoples’ Rep. of Korea’. Other relevant laws are land, environment, forests laws as well as different by-laws, regulations and operational guidelines. 

Management structure :I. MBCPC – Management Bureau of Cultural Property Conservation, under Ministry of Culture; II. BCP – Bureau of Cultural Preservation, at provincial and city levels; III. Cultural preservation departments of city, county or district; IV. CRMO – Cultural Relics Management Office, prepares and implements the conservation and management; V. Site Managers. 61 

Resources :Consists of national and local budget. 

Justification by the State Party (summary) 

Criterion i: Excellent artistic quality wall paintings depicting daily life pictures and other scenes. Important for its artistic and historic values. Outstanding architectural elements showing planning and technical skills. 

Criterion ii : The burial practice of Koguryo had an influence on that of other cultures in the region, including Japan. 

Criterion iii : The wall paintings document the history, religious beliefs, and customs of the contemporary people, as well as science and culture. They show costumes, arms, musical instruments, dance, astronomy, etc. 

Criterion iv : The nominated tombs represent an important architectural form of tombs in this region and period. 

3. ICOMOS EVALUATION 

Actions by ICOMOS 

An ICOMOS mission visited the sites between the 2 nd and 9th of July 2002. ICOMOS has consulted its International Scientific Committee on Wall Painting. 

Conservation 

State of conservation :Most of the tombs are properly maintained and well preserved. Some of the tombs suffer of deterioration of the paintings. Some are regularly flooded. Old conservation interventions seem problematic. Several tombs have special doors installed to prevent direct impact of exterior environmental conditions. 

Management :The management structure and staffing is good and qualified. There are problems with monitoring, adequate equipment and with lighting. 

Risk analysis :Lack of any alarm system. Two of the tombs are in a village and have no buffer zone. Flooding of one tomb. Future tourism – no plans for its management. 

Authenticity and integrity 

The interiors of the tombs and the mural paintings are authentic and untouched. There were some authenticity issues raised regarding the Mausoleum of King Tongmyong, certain gravestones at the Jinpha-ri tomb and entrance to Tokhung-ri tomb. These are certainly new, but are part of the presentation and interpretation of the sites – not pretending to be an authentic element, nor compromising the cultural values of the tombs. 

Comparative evaluation 

The Koguryo tombs are unique to this important culture. Therefore the only comparison can be of the different tombs of this culture to each other. It seems, comparing them also to those included in the nomination submitted by China, that a proper choice has been made. 

Outstanding universal value 

General statement: 

Due to the importance of the culture and the excellent representation of the culture by the paintings, the property meets the requirement of Outstanding Universal Value. 

Evaluation of criteria :The high significance of the property comes from the importance of the Koguryo kingdom’s culture to which the structural solutions of the tombs ceilings, as well as the testimony to daily life depicted on the wall paintings, are the only remains. The nomination meets criteria i, ii, iii and iv :

Criterion i : It is certainly a representation of special engineering genius and solutions. Its wall paintings are art masterpieces of the culture and period of the Koguryo kingdom as well as important documentation. 

Criterion ii : These special burial habits had influence on others cultures in the region, including in Japan. 

Criterion iii : The nominated tombs are a unique testimony to the important Koguryo kingdom, its culture and civilization. 

Criterion iv : The tombs, wall paintings and engineering solutions are all together an outstanding example of type of buildings and technology. The Koguryo culture had an impact on later cultures in the region, much of it represented by later, though similar type of burials (for example – in Japan). 

4. ICOMOS RECOMMENDATIONS 

Recommendation for the future 

- Strengthen modern research, including on pigments; - Prepare visitors management plan; - Install signage which will tell the history of the kingdom and sites including the fact that some sculptures at entrance to tombs are reconstructed for interpretation purposes and that the tomb of the “First King” is his second tomb, which did not house his body. - Improve monitoring equipment; - Improve lighting. 62 

Recommendation with respect to inscription 

That the property be inscribed on the World Heritage List on the basis of criteria i, ii, iii, and iv :

Criterion i : For the outstanding skills of the artist preparing the wall paintings and for ingenious engineering solutions for the construction of the tombs. 

Criterion ii : For these special burial habits had influence on others cultures in the region, including in Japan. 

Criterion iii : Being an exceptional testimony of the Koguryo culture, its burial habits as well as its daily life and beliefs. 

Criterion iv : Being an important example for burial typology. ICOMOS encourages DPR Korea and PR of China, who is also nominating a site of the Koguryan culture, to look in the future for a possibility of a joint nomination. ICOMOS decides not to get into an existing conflict of the exact dating of the culture and the tombs. While these are important scientific and cultural questions, ICOMOS believes that they have no impact on the cultural values of the nomination. ICOMOS, March 2004 74 

# Tombes de Koguryo (R. D. P. de Corée) No 1091 

1. IDENTIFICATION 

État Partie : République démocratique populaire de Corée 

Bien proposé : Ensemble des tombes de Koguryo 

Lieu : Pyongyang, province de Phyongan méridionale, Nampho, province de Hwangghae méridionale 

Date de réception : 25 janvier 2002 

Catégorie de bien : 

En termes de catégories de biens culturels telles qu’elles sont définies à l’article premier de la Convention du patrimoine mondial de 1972, il pourrait s’agir d’un 

monument . Il s’agit d’une proposition d’inscription sérielle. 

Brève description : 

Le bien est composé de plusieurs groupes de tombes et de tombes isolées datant de la période du royaume de Koguryo. Ce royaume engloba le nord-est de la Chine et la moitié de la péninsule coréenne entre le IIIe siècle avant J.-C. et le VIIe siècle apr. J.-C. et fut l’un des plus puissants de la région. Ces tombes, qui datent de la dernière période du royaume et dont beaucoup possèdent de magnifiques peintures murales, sont quasiment les seuls vestiges de cette culture. 

2. LE BIEN 

Description 

Le bien proposé pour inscription consiste en une trentaine de tombes individuelles, principalement situées dans des zones rurales et dans quelques villages. Il existe plusieurs types de tombes – empilement de pierres, chambre de pierres, et tumuli. Jusqu’à présent, plus de 10 000 de ces tombes appartenant au royaume de Koguryo ont été répertoriées en Chine et en Corée. Environ 90 d’entre elles sont décorées de peintures murales, dont 70 se trouvent en Corée et près de la moitié sont l’objet de cette proposition d’inscription. On pense que ces tombes décorées étaient destinées aux rois, aux membres de la famille royale et à d’autres aristocrates. Les peintures qui ornent les tombes sont de différents types : portraits seuls, portraits avec quatre divinités, quatre divinités seules, et motifs décoratifs. Il existe également plusieurs types de tombes, selon le nombre des chambres funéraires – chambre unique, deux chambres, plusieurs chambres et chambres secondaires. Les tombes sont construites en pierre et des couloirs mènent aux chambres funéraires. Les tombes possèdent des plafonds de formes variées dont certains, très élaborés, ont dû répondre à la nécessité de couvrir de larges espaces sans report de charge sur des colonnes et avec des dalles de pierre supportant la lourde charge d’un tumulus en pierre ou en terre. 

Histoire 

Le royaume de Koguryo dura près de 1000 ans (de 277 av. J.-C. à 668 apr. J.-C.). Il fut fondé à Huanren, dans la province du Liaoning, en Chine, puis déplacé successivement, en l’an 3 apr. J.-C., au château de Kungnae à Ji’an, dans la province de Jilin en Chine, puis en l’an 427 sur le mont Taesong, dans la province de Pyongyang, et enfin au château de Jangan au centre de la ville actuelle de Pyongyang. Située sur un lieu stratégique, Pyongyang, capitale de l’ancienne Corée (Kojoson), était depuis longtemps le centre culturel, économique et politique du royaume de Koguryo, ce qui motiva l’installation et le développement de la capitale dans ce lieu. Le royaume de Koguryo étendit son territoire jusqu’à couvrir le nord-est de la Chine et la moitié de la péninsule coréenne, devenant l’un des pouvoirs les plus puissants d’Extrême-Orient. Il s’effondra en l’an 668. Les vestiges les mieux connus de ce patrimoine culturel sont constitués de milliers de tombes construites en pierre et surmontées de tertre en pierre ou en terre. Les tumuli, dont beaucoup comportent des peintures murales, se trouvèrent en plus grand nombre à Pyongyang car le royaume de Koguryo y installa sa capitale, mais ces tombes sont loin d’être absentes d’autres régions du royaume. La plupart des tombes ont souffert de fouilles clandestines dans les mille dernières années. Très peu d’entre elles ont donc bénéficié de fouilles scientifiques avant les pillages et très peu d’ensembles d’objets complets en ont été extraits. Les tombes ont attiré l’attention internationale en 1905, pendant l’occupation japonaise, période pendant laquelle nombre d’entre elles ont été ouvertes au public. Les premières recherches scientifiques et documentaires ont été entreprises par des spécialistes japonais entre 1911 et les années 1940. Des études, des fouilles et des travaux de documentation sont entrepris régulièrement depuis 1945. Des actions de conservation mineures ont été réalisées au début des années 1940, telles que la restriction de l’accès à certaines tombes et la création d’entrée pour d’autres. Des travaux d’entretien, de protection et de conservation sont régulièrement entrepris depuis 1946, dans le cadre d’une législation adaptée et avec la désignation de gestionnaires de sites. 75 

Politique de gestion 

Dispositions légales :Les trois lois principales qui protègent et gèrent le patrimoine culturel sont les suivantes : le décret présidentiel 35, la « constitution socialiste de la République démocratique populaire de Corée » et la « loi de la République démocratique populaire de Corée ». D’autres lois concernent l’occupation des sols, l’environnement, les forêts ; des règlements et des directives s’appliquent également. 

Structure de la gestion : 

- MBCPC - Le Bureau de gestion de la conservation de biens culturels, sous la tutelle du ministère de la Culture. - BCP - Le Bureau de la préservation culturelle, au niveau des villes et des provinces. - Les services de préservation de la culture de la ville, du comté ou du district. - CRMO – Le Bureau de gestion des reliques culturelles prépare et met en œuvre les politiques de gestion et de conservation. - Les gestionnaires de site 

Ressources : 

Elles sont prélevées sur les budgets nationaux et locaux. 

Justification émanant de l’État partie (résumé) 

Critère i : Les peintures murales, d’excellente qualité artistique, dépeignent des scènes de la vie quotidienne et autres. Elles sont importantes pour leur intérêt historique et artistique. Des détails architectoniques remarquables témoignent des compétences architecturales et techniques de l’époque. 

Critère ii : Les pratiques funéraires de Koguryo eurent une influence sur celles d’autres cultures de la région, ycompris le Japon. 

Critère iii : Les peintures murales illustrent l’histoire, les croyances religieuses et les coutumes des peuples et témoignent de la science et de la culture à cette époque. Elles dépeignent des vêtements traditionnels, des armes, des instruments de musique, des danses, l’astronomie, etc. 

Critère iv : Les tombes proposées pour inscription représentent une forme architecturale funéraire importante dans la région et pour la période envisagée. 

3. ÉVALUATION DE L’ICOMOS 

Action de l’ICOMOS 

Une mission d’expertise de l’ICOMOS a visité les sites du 2 au 9 juillet 2002. L’ICOMOS a également consulté son Comité Scientifique International sur les peintures murales. 

Conservation 

État de conservation : 

La plupart des tombes sont correctement entretenues et bien préservées. Les peintures de certaines tombes souffrent parfois de dégradations. Certaines tombes subissent régulièrement des inondations. Les anciennes interventions de conservation semblent poser problème. Des portes spéciales ont été installées dans plusieurs tombes afin de prévenir les impacts directs des conditions environnementales extérieures. 

Gestion : 

La structure de la gestion est bonne et le personnel est compétent. Le suivi, le matériel approprié et l’éclairage sont sources de problèmes. 

Analyse des risques : 

Il n’y a pas de système d’alarme. Deux des tombes sont situées dans un village et ne possèdent pas de zone tampon. Une tombe est régulièrement inondée. Il n’existe pas de plan de gestion pour le tourisme à venir. 

Authenticité et intégrité 

Les intérieurs des tombes et les peintures murales sont authentiques et intacts. Des problèmes d’authenticité se sont posés pour le mausolée du roi Tongmyong, des pierres tombales de la tombe de Jinpha-ri et l’entrée de la tombe de Tokhung-ri. Ces éléments sont certes nouveaux mais font partie de la présentation et de l’interprétation des sites. Ils ne sont pas authentiques mais ne compromettent pas les valeurs culturelles des tombes. 

Évaluation comparative 

Les tombes de Koguryo sont uniques pour cette importante culture. La seule comparaison possible est donc celle que l’on peut faire entre différentes tombes de cette même culture. Il apparaît, en les comparant avec celles comprises dans la proposition d’inscription chinoise, qu’un choix approprié a été fait. 

Valeur universelle exceptionnelle 

Déclaration générale : 

En raison de l’importance de cette culture et de son excellente représentation par les peintures, le bien remplit les exigences de valeur universelle exceptionnelle .76 

Évaluation des critères : 

L’importance significative du bien découle de celle de la culture Koguryo, dont les seuls vestiges sont précisément les solutions structurelles des plafonds des tombes ainsi que les peintures murales qui témoignent de la vie quotidienne. La proposition répond aux critères i, ii, iii et iv :

Critère i : Il s’agit assurément d’une représentation du génie créateur humain. Les peintures murales sont des chef-d’œuvres de la culture et de la période du royaume de Koguryo ainsi que des témoignages précieux. 

Critère ii : Les pratiques funéraires spécifiques de Koguryo eurent une influence sur d’autres cultures de la région, y compris le Japon. 

Critère iii : Les tombes proposées pour inscription sont des témoignages uniques du grand royaume de Koguryo, de sa culture et de sa civilisation. 

Critère iv : Les tombes, les peintures murales et les solutions structurelles sont un exemple remarquable d’un type d’édifice et d’une technologie. La culture Koguryo a eu une influence sur des cultures plus tardives dans la région, illustrée pour une grande part par des types de sépultures postérieurs bien que similaires (au Japon par exemple). 

4. RECOMMANDATIONS DE L’ICOMOS 

Recommandations pour le futur 

- Renforcer la recherche actuelle, notamment sur les pigments. - Préparer le plan de gestion des visiteurs. - Installer une signalétique pour expliquer l’histoire du royaume et des sites et en indiquant que certaines sculptures à l’entrée des tombes sont des reconstructions pour des raisons d’interprétation et que la tombe du « Premier roi » est sa deuxième sépulture et ne renferme pas sa dépouille. - Améliorer le contrôle de l’équipement. - Améliorer l’éclairage. 

Recommandation concernant l’inscription 

Que le bien soit inscrit sur la Liste du patrimoine mondial sur la base des critères i, ii, iii et iv :

Critère i : Pour les compétences remarquables des artistes qui ont exécuté les peintures murales et les solutions structurelles ingénieuses qui ont été trouvées pour la construction des tombes. 

Critère ii : Pour les pratiques funéraires spécifiques de Koguryo qui eurent une influence sur d’autres cultures de la région, y compris le Japon. 

Critère iii : En tant que témoignage exceptionnel de la culture Koguryo, de ses pratiques funéraires, de sa vie quotidienne et de ses croyances. 

Critère iv : En tant qu’exemple important d’une typologie funéraire. L’ICOMOS encourage la République démocratique populaire de Corée et la République populaire de Chine, qui propose également pour inscription un site de la culture Koguryo, d’étudier dans le futur la possibilité d’une proposition d’inscription conjointe. L’ICOMOS décide de ne pas entrer dans le débat existant sur la datation exacte de la culture et des tombes. Bien que ces questions soient importantes du point de vue scientifique et culturel, l’ICOMOS pense qu’elles n’ont pas de conséquences sur les valeurs culturelles de la proposition d’inscription. ICOMOS, mars 2004
